links.comparator_used: Original customized prompt written by informaticians and tested in the Epic test environment (pre-period), versus the engineered prompt (post-period) built with perplexity-based selection, few-shot examples and self-consistency scoring against ground truth
links.outcome: Provider use of GPT-4 draft replies (primary) and provider negative sentiment ('thumbs down')
links.effect: Negative sentiment fell from 12.0% (n=468) to 8.2% (n=307), OR 0.43 (95% CI 0.36-0.52, P<.01). Unadjusted use did not differ (778 vs 549, P=.89). In the mixed model the engineered prompt was associated with lower use (beta -0.10; 95% CI -0.11 to -0.09, P<.01). Only 2.6% of messages were left identical or nearly identical.
links.tradeoff: Message use decreased despite better sentiment. Providers may have already formed opinions about draft usefulness. Use rose to 35.8% only after nurses were added with extra in-servicing and education, which was outside the primary analysis. The authors say workflow and human-factors integration is needed.
links.quote: In mixed-effects logistic regression, the odds ratio of having a negative sentiment was lower with the engineered prompt versus the original prompt with an odds ratio of 0.43 (95% CI, 0.36-0.52, P < .01).

design_hint: prompt engineering guardrails for LLM-drafted patient message replies (pre-post)
